title: Family Blue America's Family Values Aaron Renn
author: Renn, Aaron
summary: Renn's weekly digest leads with an analysis of a piece by DC resident Joshua Sohn observing a surprising mix of egalitarian and traditional markers among progressive families in his neighborhood: while every family has two working parents and few share the same last name, marriage is virtually universal, divorce nearly nonexistent, income hypergamy persists (most fathers out-earn mothers), and about a third of children attend church weekly. Renn notes this as evidence that conservative family practices show up among people who vote Democrat. He then comments on evangelical culture's failure to serve single women who desire marriage — offering no practical self-improvement advice unlike secular culture or the manosphere, which is built on self-improvement as a foundational principle. Best-of-the-web links include pieces on fatherhood brain benefits, America's fertility rate, and Ezra Klein on climate and parenthood.
points: Among blue-state elite DC families, marriage is virtually universal and divorce nearly nonexistent — challenging the narrative that family decline tracks neatly with liberal politics.
Income hypergamy remains strong in culturally egalitarian blue-city households: most fathers out-earn mothers, rarely the other way around.
Religious practice persists among progressive elite: roughly one-third of children's families attend church weekly.

Evangelical culture fails single women who desire marriage — it offers only admonitions not to be too unhappy about singleness, while the secular world and manosphere dispense practical self-improvement advice.
Conservative family values often appear in practice among people who vote Democrat — traditional family practices have market appeal independent of political alignment.
quotes: Blue families certainly do exist. I live among them... These families also have some remarkable features: marriage is virtually universal, while divorce is virtually nonexistent. Almost every kid is growing up in a two-parent married family.

Given that Blue Americans tend to favor egalitarian gender roles over traditional gender roles, you might assume that deep-Blue families in a deep-Blue city like DC fall squarely on the egalitarian side. But that's not what you see among the families in our social circle. Instead, you see a more surprising mix of egalitarian and trad lifestyle markers.
Income hypergamy is alive and well among these families. Most fathers out-earn mothers, and it's rarely the other way around.

The contrast with the messages men receive is jarring. The foundational principle of the manosphere is self-improvement. It dispenses a vast array of practical insight and advice to help men get what they want and navigate life. But the evangelical world doesn't seem to offer its single women who desire marriage much beyond admonitions not to be too unhappy about their condition.
This might be one reason that conservative elites like Sohn very frequently choose to live in deep blue areas rather than ones where they'd be surrounded by Republican voters.
